lesson.menu_desc: Defending one pricing option over another with comparatives, superlatives and degree modifiers -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 15 -- Comparing Options Under Pressure
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Marcio Ferreira Santos | Lesson 15 -- Comparing Options Under Pressure

listenings.text: Before we vote, let me put the three options side by side, because the numbers are closer than they look. Option one, the broad price cut, has the biggest upside on volume, but it is also by far the most expensive: almost two points of margin. Option two, the loyalty price, is much cheaper, and it pays back in about four months, which is more than twice as fast as option one. Its weakness is reach. Only a third of our customers use the app. Option three, doing nothing, is the cheapest option today and the most expensive one in six months, because our main competitor is already lower on forty of our top items. So my recommendation is option two, with option one as the fallback in one region. And please, nobody call the difference between them negligible. It is about one and a half points of margin.

In a case discussion at a school like Booth, the professor will often ask you to choose between two options and defend your choice in under a minute. Most people compare everything, and the answer gets longer and weaker with every sentence. A stronger answer does three things. First, it starts with the choice: I would choose option B. Second, it compares on one or two dimensions only, the ones that matter most, and it gives the size of the difference. Not cheaper, but significantly cheaper. Not faster, but twice as fast. Third, it names the biggest downside of its own option before anybody else does. That last step is the one that builds trust. A person who can say what is weak in his own recommendation sounds like someone who has already done the analysis, not someone who is selling.

extra_audio.text: First, he states his choice in one sentence. Then he compares the options on the dimension that matters most. After that, he gives the size of the difference. Next, he names the biggest downside of his own option. Finally, he says what his fallback is.
